en: Mayon Volcano builds its steep cone because thick, viscous lava cools quickly and piles up near the central vent.
Heavy rainfall in the Sierra Madre mountains causes rapid water runoff, carving deep river valleys like the Cagayan River.
The southwest monsoon brings heavy rain to the Philippines because it picks up vast moisture while crossing the warm South China Sea.
Dripping water in the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River dissolves limestone bedrock to slowly carve massive underground cave systems over millennia.
Taal Volcano erupts explosively because lake water seeps into the magma chamber, instantly flashing into high-pressure steam that blasts ash upward.
Coral reefs in Tubbataha grow because tiny coral polyps continuously secrete calcium carbonate skeletons that accumulate into massive structures over centuries.
The Banaue Rice Terraces prevent soil erosion because their stepped stone walls slow down rainwater runoff on the steep Cordillera mountains.
Lake Taal formed inside a volcanic caldera because a massive ancient eruption emptied the magma chamber, causing the ground above to collapse.
Mossy forests on Mount Apo absorb heavy monsoon rains, slowly releasing the stored water to feed local rivers during dry seasons.
The Kuroshio Current warms the eastern Philippine Sea because it continuously transports warm tropical water northward from the equatorial Pacific.
The Valley Fault System generates earthquakes because tectonic stress causes locked crustal rocks to suddenly slip and release stored seismic energy.
The northeast monsoon brings cool, dry air to the Philippines because it originates from high-pressure weather systems over cold Siberia and China.
